Title: 'Ain't no mountain high enough' for IED graduate
NewsSummary: AKU prepared me to be an educator, and not just a teacher. - Lilian Amaniyo
NewsContent:
Lillian Amaniyo was ecstatic when she received her acceptance letter from Aga Khan University in 2017. Having worked for seven years as an English teacher at a secondary school, she felt it was time to advance her skills. 

She immediately began to prepare for the long journey ahead. The Master's in Education course is offered at the Institute for Educational Development (IED) based in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Lillian's home is in Koboko town in Uganda - that's almost 2,000 kilometres away - but she didn't want anything to hold her back. 

"I had seen a difference in AKU graduates - they were not just teaching for the sake of it, they were doing much more. This is when I knew that I needed to pursue my postgraduate education at IED," she said.

With support from her husband Simon Adoke, an alumni of IED, Lillian knew her four children would be well taken care of. He rallied behind her making sure she had everything she needed to concentrate on her studies by paying for her bus ticket and other travel necessities.

Lillian bid her family goodbye and hopped on to a bus. It was a ten-hour ride to the capital Kampala, and another 48-hour ride to Dar es Salaam. When she arrived at the Tanzanian capital, she was tired but relieved and excited to join the programme.

"I had very supporting classmates. They made sure I settled in well, comforted me when I missed home and made me enjoy my time both in and out of school. My roommate Veronica, was like a sister to me. We studied, cooked and even went shopping together."

She also got a scholarship from IED, meaning that a huge chunk of her worries was cut off.

"When I received the scholarship letter, I was lost for words. It meant an opportunity of a lifetime. I financed my undergraduate studies and it was hard, especially when money was tight. I don't think I'd have pursued a postgraduate degree if it wasn't for the scholarship."

It was an intense year of learning, with the support of faculty and a wide access to information through e-learning and a fully stocked library. She credits IED faculty, Dr Samuel Andema for his support to this day, which she says contributed to her growth as an educator. 

Lillian specialized in Language and Literacy, which has always been her passion since teaching Form 3 and 5 students back home in Koboko, Uganda. She had to stretch her initial limits and get into research, which was a crucial step to completing the programme.

"I co-presented a research paper at the 6th Annual Research Institute conference in 2019. This experience made me realise that research is not just an obligation for attaining a degree, but finding solutions to educational challenges, more so translating research into practice."

In February 2020, Lillian will join the AKU alumni family - a credit she is immensely proud of. She is currently an Assistant Education Officer at a local secondary school in Uganda and hopes to pursue a PhD in future. 

"AKU prepared me to be an educator, and not just a teacher."
